newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says misunderstandings with Moscow ended.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says misunderstandings with Moscow ended.

text.p: Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan returned from a four-day visit to Russia on Friday, saying his trip had cleared away Soviet-era misunderstandings with Moscow.

He told a news conference that Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif was likely to visit early next year and he also conveyed Sharif's invitation for Russian President Boris Yeltsin to visit Pakistan.

Khan said Russia supported Pakistan's proposal for Afghan peace talks in Islamabad under U.N. auspices with participation by Afghanistan's immediate neighbours as well as Russia and the United States to stand as guarantors for any peace agreement.
He said Islamabad had "excellent" relations with Moscow from 1965 to 1969, when his late father Field Marshal Ayub Khan was Pakistani president, but added that misunderstandings cropped up later.
He called his talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov "very fruitful" and said: "We were able ... to clear some misunderstandings that had cropped up in the past."

Khan declined to specify the misunderstandings, but he seemed to refer to Moscow's close political and military ties with Pakistan's arch-foe India and the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, which Pakistan opposed.

Islamabad's ties with Moscow improved after the then Soviet Union mediated an India-Pakistan peace accord after their war in September 1966, but worsened during the Indo-Pakistan war over Bangladesh in 1970, when Islamabad accused Moscow of aiding India.
The relations between the two sides were at their lowest ebb during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, when Pakistan played host to guerrilla groups fighting the Russians.
Khan said he had found Primakov "very forthcoming" about Pakistan's desire to restore the ties with Russia to the 1965-69 level and "place behind us all the misunderstandings".
He said the two sides would seek to promote presently insignificant trade and Russia showed interest in bidding for development projects in Pakistan.

Khan said that during his visit to Moscow he had signed three agreements -- on consular matters, cultural cooperation and drug trafficking -- and that half a dozen more would be ready for Sharif's visit next year.
